author: reek
body: The console editor can save a file, and this is the test that says so. Until now editor-save called write-file, which stopped being a builtin and was never replaced, so the name resolved nowhere: ConsoleEditor died with CDX3002 and every chapter citing it died with it. The whole repository-protocol surface was dark behind one undefined name.

author: reek
body: The claim this pins is narrower and more useful than "it compiles". This program holds FileSystem.Read and FileSystem.Write and it holds NOTHING else -- no Device.Block. editor-save performs write-file as a bare effect op, so the compiler's default servicer picks it up, checks the granted direction bit, elevates, and drives fat16 on this program's behalf. So a save through the editor is a save through the FileSystem layer, and holding the layer never grants the disk.

author: reek
body: The grant is unscoped because editor-save is unscoped, and that is not an oversight in either place: an editor saves the path the user opened, so the function genuinely may touch anything. A scoped grant here is refused at compile time (CDX4002 -- the checker will not let a narrow grant service an unscoped performer), which is the scope machinery working. Scoping belongs to the application that mounts the editor, not to the editor.

author: reek
body: The read-back shares no code with the writer: read-text goes through the servicer to fat16-read-text, which walks the directory and follows the cluster chain. A save that reported success and wrote nothing would pass a test that only looked at editor-save's own answer, so this one looks at the bytes that came back off the volume instead.

author: reek
body: The same buffer aimed at a subdirectory. This is the assertion that used to pin the OTHER half of the story: fat16-create-file refused any name with a path separator, so this save failed, and the point of pinning it was that it failed HONESTLY -- the editor reported the failure instead of reporting a save that never happened, which is what the old write-file builtin did.

author: reek
body: That gap is closed now, and this line is what said so: it was written as a tripwire, and it tripped. fat16-create-in-subdir resolves the parent with the read side's own walk and hands a byte address to the same create-at-slot the root uses, so the save lands. The disk fixture carries a real /SUB directory built host-side from the FAT16 spec (build/make-fat16-subdir.ps1).

author: reek
body: What this now proves is the whole stack in one line: the editor performs a bare write-file effect op, the compiler's default servicer picks it up, elevates, and drives fat16 into a subdirectory -- while this program holds FileSystem and never Device.Block.

author: reek
body: A path whose parent does not exist is still refused, and still refused honestly. That is the tripwire's replacement: the capability grew, so the assertion moved to the edge of what is still true rather than being deleted.
